item.content:encoded:
This article strikes me as being incomplete. The rings turn people into perfectly nice spouses… and they also cause deaths? How?? A perfectly nice spouse wouldn't commit murder or suicide, ever. The enslaved person might be miserable, yes, but if a ring is fully controlling your mind then you can't do anything about your misery but experience it. You can't flip out and murder your partner.

Or can you? Presumably the control of the ring can be broken if the slave is very VERY miserable?? Or maybe, in practice, a ring simply comes off by accident once in a while, and then the slave finally gets a chance to express his/her misery? These ideas are perfectly plausible. But the article doesn't say which ones (if any) are correct. This is basic, crucial information about how the anomalous item works! It obviously needs to be in there.

I wonder what it does to non-adults. How does it define an adult in the first place; calendar age and local cultural norms, self-image, medical post-pubescence?
How does it define "in a relationship"? And how would it react to polygamy or friends-with-benefits situations?
How does it react to subjects with different cultural standards of the perfect spouse? Would a jungle tribe that had never heard of June and Ward Cleaver still get the Stepford personas; or would it draw on the local meme-plex of what a wife should be?

What I'm getting at is that there are other variables to be explored with as much scientific rigor as shown for gender and orientation. And I think it could make for a good read.

Could be enough meat there for a separate testing log.

what does 'assigned male at birth' mean? That someone is biologically male? What if a gender-ambiguous (i.e hermaphroditical) child was born, and no identity was 'assigned' to them?

item.content:encoded:
Really not a fan. The tone is all wrong, frequently using very un-scientific language such as "good with kids" and generally it's just… too goofy, and I usually don't mind goofy SCPs, and the attempt to make it dark with the domestic abuse stuff just doesn't work for me. Plus, the including of a famous character like DR. Rights feels forced.

Also, a big pet peeve of mine which is not specific to this article but is present here so I might as well point it out…

They are relatively plain, and bear no marks as to their origin or make, but staff routinely describe them as seeming like "very nice wedding rings, if a little plain."

I keep seeing it and it's driving me up the wall: stop using direct quotes to describe SCPs. Why, oh why would a scientist writing a report on an SCP, which is supposed to be completely objective and stick to the facts, do this?

It adds no information relevant to the containment or study of the SCP and it is a complete shift from the clinical tone of the reports.

It's especially bad when you have descriptions this specific because it implies that EVERY person questioned on the subject used the exact same sentence, which is ludicrous. It'd be one thing if it were a memetic effect of the SCP but it never is.

Just… stop doing it, people, please. It's unnecessary, it comes across as poor writing and it destroys suspension of disbelief. It just makes it look like the author wanted to give us a specific description but couldn't put it in a way that works in-universe so they just up and told us directly. Guys, even in written media, "show, don't tell" remains an important guideline for convincing world-building.
